title: Chemistry everywhere
summary: Learn about cleaning products, polymers, medicines, food and farm chemistry.
cards.0.p: Every day in the kitchen and bathroom you use chemicals such as salt, baking soda, vinegar and bleach. Cleaning products, plastics, medicines and food additives are all chemistry too. That's why you should read the label.
cards.0.key: Baking soda is NaHCO₃, washing soda is Na₂CO₃ and slaked lime is Ca(OH)₂. Muriatic acid is an HCl solution.
cards.0.once.soru: What is the chemical name of the soda used to make a cake rise?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Baking soda is NaHCO₃. When heated it releases CO₂ and makes the dough rise.
cards.1.p: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a fatty acid. The tail of a soap molecule sinks into the grease, and the head faces the water. The sphere that forms this way is called a micelle. The micelle keeps dirt suspended in water.
cards.1.etk.soru: Tap the parts of the soap molecule and the micelle.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.0.acik: The tail is a long hydrocarbon chain. It is nonpolar, so it loves grease, not water.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.1.acik: The head is the ionic −COO⁻ end. It interacts well with polar water molecules.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.2.acik: Nonpolar grease does not dissolve in water. The soap's tails sink into the grease.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.3.acik: Water molecules surround the heads on the micelle's surface. This keeps the dirt suspended in water.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.4.acik: A polar solvent. The micelles carrying dirt spread through the water and rinse away.
cards.1.key: The ionic head loves water (hydrophilic) and the hydrocarbon tail loves grease (hydrophobic). Soap is made from fat and NaOH (with glycerol as a byproduct).
cards.2.p: Hard water contains a lot of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺. Soap forms an insoluble scum with these ions and lathers poorly. When hard water is heated, CaCO₃ settles out, and this is how limescale forms in a kettle.
cards.2.svg#1: heating temporary hard water deposits limescale
cards.2.key: Temporary hardness from Ca(HCO₃)₂ goes away when you boil the water. Permanent hardness from CaSO₄ does not.
cards.3.p: Detergents are synthetic cleaners made from petroleum, and their structure is similar to soap. They don't form scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, so they lather even in hard water.
cards.3.key: The head group of a detergent is −SO₃⁻. Soap breaks down more easily in nature. Detergents with phosphates can cause excess algae growth in lakes.
cards.4.p: When bleach mixes with acid, toxic Cl₂ gas is released (NaOCl + 2HCl → NaCl + H₂O + Cl₂). When bleach mixes with an ammonia cleaner, toxic chloramine forms.
cards.4.svg#15: Both are toxic: they burn the airways.
cards.4.key: Acidic limescale removers also release chlorine when mixed with bleach. Use cleaning products one at a time. If you notice a sharp chlorine smell, leave the room at once and open the windows.
cards.5.p: A polymer is a giant molecule made by joining thousands of small monomers. Ethene gives polyethylene (bags), vinyl chloride gives PVC (pipes), and tetrafluoroethene gives Teflon.
cards.5.key: PET, which water bottles are made of, is made from two different monomers. Plastics are synthetic polymers. Starch, cellulose and proteins are natural polymers. You'll see the details in the Hydrocarbons topic.
cards.6.p: The number inside the triangle on a plastic shows its type. 1 is PET, 2 HDPE, 3 PVC, 5 PP and 6 PS. Plastics stay in nature for hundreds of years and break into microplastics.
cards.6.svg#22: The number in the triangle shows the plastic type.
cards.6.key: 4 is LDPE and 7 is other. The triangle does not guarantee that it will be recycled. Biodegradable plastics (such as PLA made from starch) are broken down by microorganisms under the right conditions.
cards.6.once.soru: What happens to a plastic bottle thrown into the sea?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Plastic breaks down very slowly in nature. It crumbles into microplastics.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.yazi: It rots in a few months
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Microorganisms can't break down most plastics.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: Plastics are nonpolar, so they don't dissolve in water.
cards.7.p: The substance that makes a medicine work is called the active ingredient. Too small a dose does nothing, and too much is poisonous. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses.
cards.7.key: The same active ingredient can be sold under different brand names. If antibiotics are misused or stopped early, resistant bacteria multiply. So take an antibiotic for as long as the doctor says.
cards.7.once.soru: What happens if someone with the flu takes an antibiotic?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The flu is a viral disease, and antibiotics act only on bacteria. Unnecessary use leads to resistance.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: An antibiotic gives no immunity, because it is not a vaccine.
cards.8.p: Food spoils because of microorganisms, enzymes and oxygen. Cooling, drying, salting and pasteurization slow spoilage down. Additives are listed on the label with E numbers.
cards.8.key: Fats go rancid when they oxidize. Preservatives, colors and antioxidants are all additives. An E number shows that an additive is permitted. But it doesn't mean you can eat unlimited amounts.
cards.8.once.soru: How does salt in brine keep food from spoiling?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Concentrated salt draws water out of microorganisms by osmosis. So the microorganisms can't multiply.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Oxygen speeds up spoilage, and salt does not add oxygen.
cards.9.p: The values on a nutrition label are usually per 100 g. The use-by date is a safety limit, and the best-before date is about quality.
cards.9.key: The label lists energy, fat, saturated fat, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt. If you eat the whole pack, do the math for the pack's mass. On cosmetics, the ingredients are listed from most to least.
cards.10.p: Fertilizer gives plants nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Pesticides kill pests. Insecticides are used against insects, herbicides against weeds and fungicides against fungi. Too much fertilizer causes eutrophication in lakes.
cards.10.svg#11: pesticides build up along the food chain
cards.10.key: Persistent pesticides such as DDT build up as they move up the food chain. Predators are affected the most.
cards.10.once.soru: Rain carries excess fertilizer from a field into a lake. What happens in the lake?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: Fertilizer feeds the algae too. As the algae rot, the oxygen in the water drops and the fish die.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Fertilizer pollutes the water, and the excess nutrients upset the balance.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The oxygen drops, so the fish die.
cards.11.h: Check the pH when choosing a product
cards.11.p: Limescale is a basic deposit, and an acidic product (vinegar) dissolves it. Greasy dirt comes off with a basic product (soap, baking soda). Never put acid on marble or strong base on aluminum.
cards.11.svg#15: limescale → acidic product · grease → basic product
cards.11.key: Skin care products have a pH close to 5.5. A stronger product is not a better one. Choose the mildest product that does the job.
cards.11.once.soru: Which removes limescale stains in the shower most easily?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: Limescale is CaCO₃, and the acid in vinegar dissolves it.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: Soap is basic. It removes greasy dirt, but it does not dissolve limescale.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Baking soda is basic too, and it does not dissolve limescale.
cards.12.p:
• Soap is a fatty acid salt, and it carries dirt into water by forming micelles.
• In hard water soap forms scum, but detergent lathers.
• Never mix bleach with acidic or ammonia cleaners.
• Plastic is a polymer and lasts a long time in nature.
• Watch the dose of medicines and read food labels.
quiz.0.q: Match each farm chemical to its job.
quiz.0.e: Insecticides, herbicides and fungicides are pesticides used against insects, weeds and fungi. Fertilizer doesn't kill pests. It gives plants nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
quiz.1.q: Sort each property under soap or detergent.
quiz.1.e: Soap is the Na or K salt of a fatty acid. It forms scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ and breaks down more easily in nature. Detergent is a synthetic substance made from petroleum, and it lathers in hard water too. Detergents with added phosphate can cause algae growth in lakes.
quiz.2.q: A bag of chips says 0.8 g of salt per 100 g. If you eat the whole 30 g bag, how many grams of salt do you get?
quiz.2.e: The values on the label are per 100 g. So 0.8 × 30 / 100 = 0.24 g of salt.
quiz.3.q: Someone mixes bleach with an ammonia glass cleaner to clean the windows. What happens?
quiz.3.o.2: They neutralize to salt and water
quiz.3.e: Hypochlorite reacts with ammonia and forms chloramine gases that burn the airways. Never mix bleach with acid or with ammonia.
quiz.3.y.1: Mixing two cleaners doesn't clean better. Together these two produce a toxic gas.
quiz.3.y.2: Ammonia is a weak base and bleach is basic too. What happens here is not neutralization but chloramine formation.
quiz.3.y.3: NaOCl reacts with ammonia and releases toxic chloramine.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Test soap, hard water, plastics and labels yourself.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Greasy dirt doesn't dissolve in water. One end of a soap molecule loves water and the other loves grease. Add soap to the water and watch how the molecules surround the grease drop.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which part of the soap molecule sinks into the greasy dirt?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The head loves water (hydrophilic). So when a micelle forms, the heads stay outside and face the water.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The tail loves grease (hydrophobic) and sinks into the dirt. The head stays outside and faces the water.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The two ends of the molecule behave differently. One loves water and the other loves grease. That is what makes soap useful.
A:adimlar.1.metin: When hard water is heated, CaCO₃ settles at the bottom of the kettle. This is the limescale you know.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: What happens if you put vinegar in a kettle with limescale?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Vinegar doesn't leave scale. On the contrary, the acid in vinegar reacts with the scale.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Vinegar is an acid (acetic acid) and limescale is a carbonate. These two react.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: CaCO₃ dissolves in acid, forming a soluble salt, water and CO₂ gas. That is why descalers are acidic.
A:adimlar.2.metin: This water contains a lot of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, and the soap lathers poorly. Change the cleaner and get lots of lather in hard water.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: Keep the water hard. Change only the cleaner.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: Synthetic detergent doesn't form scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, so it lathers in hard water too.
A:adimlar.3.metin: You might think of mixing two cleaners to clean the bathroom better. What happens when bleach (NaOCl) and muriatic acid (HCl) mix?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: What happens if you mix bleach and muriatic acid?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: NaOCl and HCl react and release toxic Cl₂ gas. This gas burns the airways. Use cleaners separately and air out the room.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Mixing doesn't clean better. The two substances react and produce a toxic gas.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: This mixture doesn't just neutralize. Chlorine gas is released too.
A:adimlar.4.metin: A polymer forms when small monomers link together like a chain. Change the monomer and make Teflon, which is used in nonstick pans.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: Tetrafluoroethene gives Teflon (PTFE). The C–F bonds are very strong and nonpolar, so almost nothing sticks to Teflon.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The values on a nutrition label are usually per 100 g. 100 g of this biscuit contains 25 g of sugar. How much do you have to eat to reach the recommended daily limit of 50 g of sugar?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: 200 g × 25 / 100 = 50 g of sugar. Scale the value on the label to the mass you eat. On cosmetics, too, ingredients are listed from most to least.
A:kapanis.0: Soap is a fatty acid salt. Its tail sinks into dirt, its head faces water, and the micelle that forms carries dirt through water.
A:kapanis.1: In hard water (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺) soap forms scum, but detergent lathers. Limescale (CaCO₃) dissolves in acid.
A:kapanis.2: Never mix bleach with acidic or ammonia cleaners, because a toxic gas is released.
A:kapanis.3: Plastics are synthetic polymers made from monomers, and they last a long time in nature.
A:kapanis.4: Label values are per 100 g. When taking medicine, follow the dose and the length of use.
